newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sears chief under pressure after sale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sears chief under pressure after sale.

text.p: Struggling British retailer Sears Plc on Monday tried to placate disgruntled investors with the sale of its Freemans mail order arm plus the promise of a 410 million pound ($686 million) cash handout.
But analysts said embattled chief executive Liam Strong's job was still on the line for failing to revive the sprawling shoes-to-Selfridges retail empire after five years at the helm.
They said investors wanted more radical solutions, including ditching the struggling British Shoe Corporation or a possible demerger of Selfridges, the group's star profit performer.
Analysts said a growing number of institutional investors were baying for Strong's blood but the lack of an obvious successor might give him breathing space in the short run.
"There's little chance of him going until they've found an adequate successor," said one retail analyst who asked to remain anonymous.
Strong's failure to deliver was highlighted last week when Sears warned that annual profits would be less than last year's 100.1 million pounds after a disappointing Christmas.
Strong, formerly marketing director at British Airways, was brought in in 1992 to transform the sluggish retail conglomerate.
But investors' patience has worn thin as his efforts to shake up the group have not delivered profit growth and its shares, currently standing one pence up at 89 pence, are still underperforming.

The poor showing has prompted renewed calls for a break up of the group to realise value from the highly profitable Selfridges department store and women's fashion chains, with well known brands such as Warehouse and Wallis.
But some retail analysts said even a break-up looked unattractive, pointing to the experience of Hanson Plc, whose demergers did not solve the problem of share price underperformance.
"Sears' break-up valuation is not hugely more than the price now," said one retail analyst.

After selling Freemans, investors now want Strong to take the knife to Sears' ailing British Shoe Corporation, which has seen sales fall nearly three percent so far in the second half of the current year in a difficult British footwear market.
"Our footwear trading performance over the next 12 months is crucial in terms of determining the potential of the footwear business for Sears," Strong said in a statement.
Industry sources said Sears could struggle to offload the business and any deal could mean a sizeable hit on the balance sheet, although BSC's property portfolio might be an attraction.
Footwear, with annual sales of up to 600 million pounds, has around 500 shops and concessions in some 250 department stores.

Strong has already introduced new formats Shoe Express and Shoe City but efforts to sell the unwanted stores were hampered last year when shops sold to privately-owned retailer Facia had to be taken back after Facia collapsed.

There is also pressure on Strong to float Selfridges, the London department store valued at between 590 and 650 million pounds. But industry sources said there were no immediate plans to spin off what was the most profitable part of the group.
Sears said the sale of Freemans to Littlewoods Organisation for 395 million pounds ($664 million) in cash would bring savings of about four million pounds per year.

The group also said it was developing a structure to return about 410 million pounds in cash to ordinary shareholders in some six months' time and expected to give further details in April of the plan. ($1=.5974 Pound)
